q-7551: Correct answer: B. The recovery position is used for an unconscious person who is breathing and has no visible injuries — it protects the airway from the tongue falling back and from stomach contents. If breathing is absent, resuscitation is started immediately.
q-7698: Correct answer: A. Heavy bleeding is stemmed with a pressure dressing: sterile material is placed on the wound, pressed down with an additional layer and bandaged firmly. An ordinary dressing quickly soaks through, and pouring antiseptics over the wound will not stop the bleeding.
q-7699: Correct answer: B. With a suspected spinal injury the injured person is left in the vehicle until the rescuers arrive. The exception is an immediate threat to life, for example fire or absence of breathing — then evacuation is necessary despite the risk.
q-7701: Correct answer: A. Tilting the head back with a nosebleed is a mistake — the blood runs down the throat and risks choking and vomiting. The head is tilted forward, the sides of the nose are pinched, and a cold compress may be applied to the back of the neck.
q-7702: Correct answer: A. Bleeding from the forearm is stemmed with a sterile dressing, a bandage and additional pressure, for example from a roll of bandage, and the limb is raised above the level of the heart. Soaked dressings are not removed — further layers are added.
q-7703: Correct answer: C. With a suspected limb fracture, the site of the injury itself and the two neighbouring joints — below and above the fracture — are immobilised. Only that extent blocks movement of the fragments and reduces pain and the risk of further damage.
q-7705: Correct answer: C. A burn is cooled with clean, cool water until the pain subsides, and then covered with a loose sterile dressing. Smearing with fat and tight bandaging deepen the injury and hinder later treatment.
q-7706: Correct answer: A. Resuscitation is stopped when the casualty begins to breathe on their own, and also when rescuers take over or the rescuer is exhausted. The mere sight of an approaching ambulance, or a set amount of time passing, is no reason to stop.
